subtitle: Prepare a conversation about race and equity that stays focused on the work. You will examine the different accounts people bring and turn discussion into responsible action.
scope: For leaders, supervisors and staff who facilitate DHS work discussions. This optional practice does not qualify a facilitator, establish personnel findings or replace required equity analysis, formal reporting or investigation. Staff own their work and may seek consultant guidance. Use practice details in learning responses; actual workplace and service information belongs in approved channels. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are outside this course and go to the appropriate office within ADSA (Aging and Disability Services Administration).
introTranscript: Conversations about race and equity need a clear purpose and a practical connection to the work. Avoiding the topic can leave a barrier unexamined; a poorly prepared discussion can also leave people carrying an unfair burden or unsure what will happen next. A leader’s role is to make the question understandable, support participation, distinguish evidence from assumptions and retain responsibility for a suitable next action. In this course you will practice preparing a discussion about a service decision, responding to an uncertain claim, making room for different experiences and addressing a problematic remark. You will distinguish a learning conversation from a formal workplace concern and develop follow-through that can be checked. Respectful inquiry does not require agreement with every statement, compulsory personal disclosure or a judgment about someone’s intercultural development.

lessons.title: Begin with the work question and the real choice
lessons.summary: Connect discussion of race and equity to a decision participants can understand and influence.
lessons.objective: Write a specific work question that allows a racial equity concern to be examined.
objectives: Write a specific work question that allows a racial equity concern to be examined.
Identify what remains open and who owns a practice decision.
Distinguish inquiry about a process from a demand for personal disclosure.
takeaways: Explain the decision and the question before inviting discussion.
Name race when relevant without assigning motives or group scripts.
A conversation must have an honest connection to action.
lessons.statement: A useful purpose makes it possible to examine race and equity without turning participants into the subject of an improvised assessment.

image.caption: A focused work question helps a group connect discussion with a decision.

intro.heading: What do we need to understand?
intro.body:
A leader wants to discuss equity in a service contact process. “Let us talk about race” may express an important intention, but it does not tell participants what the discussion will do. The team may need to understand why people do not receive understandable information, whose experience is missing or how a proposed change could affect different communities. Begin with the work question and its decision context. Explain what can change, which parts are fixed and who is responsible for the next decision.

Do not remove race from a question merely because it is uncomfortable. A racial pattern, account of exclusion or history relevant to the process may warrant careful examination. At the same time, do not assume that race explains every observed difference or that everyone assigned to a demographic category shares the same experience. State what is known, how it is known and what needs further inquiry. “We see a difference in this approved report and need to examine the process” is more useful than declaring a cause before the evidence supports it.

Participants need a genuine reason to contribute. If the decision is already final, do not call the meeting shared design of that decision. An information session or a discussion about future improvements can still be worthwhile when its purpose is accurate. If an option remains open, explain how input will be examined and how people will receive a response. A leader cannot promise to adopt every suggestion, but can take responsibility for a reasoned account of the decision.

Frame the invitation around relevant work experience and evidence. Staff should not have to disclose family history, identity experiences or a trauma account to earn a place in the discussion. No person is the representative of every member of a racial or cultural community. Offer suitable ways to contribute to the actual question, including a practice example when the purpose is learning.

This course supports that practical inquiry. DHS equity responsibilities and required analysis continue to apply under actual policy. A group conversation is not a substitute for the appropriate toolkit, authorized review or formal reporting. The consultant can help the group prepare questions and examine its reasoning; the people responsible for the work still carry out the analysis and follow-through.

inThisLesson: State the open choices and constraints.
Separate evidence from a proposed explanation.
lessons.keyStatement: Begin with a decision people can recognize and an honest account of how the discussion can matter.

flashcards.back: A specific issue about a service, decision or workplace arrangement that the group can examine.
What a record, event or account actually establishes, separated from an interpretation.
An explanation proposed for an observation; it needs examination rather than automatic acceptance.
An appropriate way to contribute without an invented requirement to share private experiences.
Supporting the purpose, participation and process of a discussion without replacing the responsible decision-maker.
The action, owner and review that connect a discussion to work.

items.title: A topic without a question
items.body: A broad subject can invite an important conversation while still leaving people uncertain about the task. Identify the process and decision it relates to. For example, ask what barriers a proposed contact route may create and what evidence is needed to compare alternatives. This gives the discussion a direction without predetermining its answer.

items.title: A decision without an open choice
items.body: If a rule cannot be changed by the team, explain that limit. Participants may still examine instructions or raise an issue through the appropriate route. Do not invite them to redesign a requirement the group lacks authority to alter. An honest boundary is more respectful than promising influence and later dismissing the work as outside scope.

items.title: A perspective without a burden
items.body: Invite relevant experience without requiring someone to speak for a whole community. Ask what they wish to contribute to the work question and provide an appropriate alternative response path. The facilitator still needs to seek other relevant evidence and perspectives. One person’s participation cannot certify that every affected experience has been heard.

tabs.label: Understand
tabs.body: An inquiry asks what is happening and what may explain it. A racial pattern can be named while causes remain uncertain. The next step may be further research or appropriate listening. This purpose works when the team genuinely needs knowledge; it should not be presented as a final finding or a vote on another person’s experience.

tabs.label: Develop options
tabs.body: An options discussion compares possible changes while a decision remains open. Explain constraints and how input will be considered. Participants can examine barriers and tradeoffs without owning the final authorization. A concrete comparison helps the group contribute to the work rather than endorse an already chosen result.

tabs.label: Explain a decision
tabs.body: An information session communicates what was decided, why and what follows. It may also gather questions or future improvement ideas. Calling it joint design misstates the current opportunity. State its purpose honestly so participants know what can still change and where a concern about the completed decision belongs.

check.question: A leader invites staff to redesign a completed decision but cannot change it. What should be corrected?
check.correct: Explain the actual purpose and limits, and identify any genuine question or future decision still open to input.
wrong: Keep the joint-design label so staff feel included.
Require staff of color to supply personal stories to justify reopening the decision.
Treat meeting attendance as proof that everyone supports the result.
check.feedbackCorrect: An honest invitation gives people a usable role without exaggerating influence or demanding private disclosure.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A welcoming label cannot create influence over a completed decision. Personal stories must not become an invented condition for being heard, and attendance cannot establish agreement. Clarify the purpose and real choices, then explain the appropriate route for other concerns.

items.text: Which contact option may create an access barrier?
What evidence is missing before we compare alternatives?
Participants may use a practice example rather than a personal account.
The team can revise instructions but cannot change the underlying rule.
Attending the discussion proves endorsement of the decision.
One colleague represents every person in a racial community.

lessons.next: Next, prepare a discussion arrangement people can actually use.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Amira schedules a discussion after approving a new service contact process. The invitation says staff will design the decision together, but Amira can only revise the explanatory instructions. A colleague asks what part remains open. Another proposes inviting one employee to provide the experience of an entire racial community. The consultant offers to help clarify the question, while Amira remains responsible for the work.
scenario.prompt: What is the strongest preparation step?
options: Keep the broad invitation and ask the employee to validate the whole design.
Revise the purpose to examine the open instructions, explain decision limits and invite scoped evidence without a representative burden.
Declare all discussion of race outside the work because the main decision is complete.
responses: The invitation overstates authority and makes one person carry a role they cannot fulfill.
This creates an honest work question and respects how people may contribute. It does not erase concerns needing another route.
Race may remain relevant to the instructions or a concern about the decision. A scope boundary should clarify the route rather than forbid inquiry.

lessons.transfer: Using an invented decision, write a work question, the choices still open, the decision owner and one participation choice.

move.control: You can make the invitation accurate and keep the question connected to the work.
move.failure: The group discusses a vague topic or offers work that the decision owner cannot use.
move.next: Before the next relevant discussion, explain what input can influence and how a response will be given.

lessons.title: Prepare participation and useful boundaries
lessons.summary: Plan access, roles, discussion expectations and appropriate alternatives before asking people to contribute.
lessons.objective: Identify preparation gaps that make a practice discussion harder to use.
objectives: Identify preparation gaps that make a practice discussion harder to use.
Write a practical conversation expectation tied to participation rather than a prescribed feeling.
Explain an appropriate pause or alternative without abandoning the work question.
takeaways: Preparation concerns actual participation, not a promise that no discomfort will occur.
Respectful boundaries protect inquiry without requiring personal agreement.
Formal concerns and private information need their proper routes.
lessons.statement: People need to understand the purpose, participation options and limits before a difficult conversation begins.

image.caption: Preparation includes checking whose participation the arrangement supports.

intro.heading: Make the arrangement workable
intro.body:
A thoughtful question can still be difficult to use when participants receive no context, the pace leaves no room to respond or the materials are inaccessible. Preparation is part of the facilitator’s work. Explain the purpose and relevant information in advance where appropriate. Ask what arrangements support participation through the responsible access process. Do not assume that sending the same document to everyone establishes an equivalent opportunity to examine it.

Clarify the roles. The facilitator supports the process and attention to the question. The decision owner explains constraints and remains responsible for the resulting work. Participants may bring knowledge, question a claim or consider alternatives. The consultant can offer preparation and feedback without becoming the person who must do every staff analysis. If the subject needs more expertise or support than the facilitator has, seek an appropriate co-facilitator or responsible guidance rather than treating authority as competence.

Agree on expectations expressed as actions. Listen to the actual statement before responding. Challenge an idea through its reasoning and evidence. Avoid assigning motives from someone’s identity or requiring them to educate others about private experiences. Explain how the group will manage interruptions and how someone can raise a process concern. “Everyone must feel comfortable” is not an expectation the facilitator can enforce or verify. People may experience uncertainty while a discussion remains respectful and useful.

Participation choices depend on the real work context. A learning exercise can use practice material and an appropriate option to pause or respond differently. Actual assigned work and required processes have their own duties. Do not invent a rule that declining personal disclosure means declining the work, or that an informal conversation must occur before a person can use a formal concern route. Explain the difference rather than making blanket promises about every meeting.

Address information limits honestly. Do not promise absolute confidentiality in a workplace discussion; records and reporting responsibilities may apply. Keep unnecessary personnel or service details out of shared material. If an allegation or specialized concern appears, use the responsible process instead of collecting accounts for a group judgment. A well-prepared discussion can preserve a valuable general question while routing an individual matter appropriately.

lessons.keyStatement: Prepare for respectful participation and uncertainty without requiring a particular emotional response.

items.title: The packet arrives at the meeting
items.body: Participants may need time or an accessible arrangement to make sense of the evidence. Offer context and usable material at an appropriate point before discussion. Ask what is needed through responsible channels rather than judging slow response as resistance. If the schedule prevents meaningful participation, revisit the arrangement with the decision owner instead of declaring silence consent.

items.title: The leader promises perfect safety
items.body: The leader can establish conduct expectations and respond to problems, but cannot guarantee another person’s feelings or prevent every uncomfortable moment. Explain what participants can expect the facilitator to do. A concrete interruption and concern route is more useful than reassurance that discourages someone from identifying a problem when the promised experience is not met.

items.title: The group collects private accounts
items.body: A vivid story can also expose information that does not belong in a shared discussion. Prepare practice or appropriately non-identifying material for learning. If someone raises a real concern, pause unnecessary detail and explain the proper route. Do not make a personal account the entry ticket for a relevant perspective or promise that the group can resolve it.

tabs.label: Continue
tabs.body: Continue when the process remains suitable and the issue can be examined within the group’s purpose. Clarify a misunderstood term or restate a neutral question rather than abandoning inquiry at the first sign of disagreement. Check participation and evidence, not whether everyone seems cheerful. Respectful discomfort can accompany useful work without authorizing personal attacks.

tabs.label: Pause
tabs.body: Pause when an interruption, access barrier or harmful exchange prevents useful participation. Explain the reason and an appropriate next arrangement. A pause is not a finding about anyone’s motives, nor an excuse to leave a concern unattended. The facilitator still owns follow-through on the process and any actual duties that arise.

tabs.label: Use another route
tabs.body: Another route is necessary when the matter exceeds the discussion’s authority or needs formal handling. Explain where the concern belongs and retain a suitable general work question if possible. An informal meeting cannot investigate a discrimination allegation by group vote. Referral should support the person and responsibility, rather than make a difficult subject disappear.

check.question: A facilitator says participants must disclose personal racial experiences before commenting on a service process. What is the better arrangement?
check.correct: Invite relevant work evidence and perspectives with suitable alternatives, without making private disclosure a condition of contribution.
wrong: Keep the requirement because personal stories always provide the best evidence.
Forbid any discussion of experience so the conversation stays impersonal.
Promise absolute confidentiality and then collect detailed personnel accounts.
check.feedbackCorrect: The group can learn from voluntarily offered perspectives without imposing disclosure or exaggerated information promises.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Personal stories are not automatically the only or strongest evidence and cannot be compelled to validate participation. Forbidding experience loses relevant knowledge, while an absolute confidentiality promise may be inaccurate. Use scoped evidence, appropriate choices and the actual information-handling route.

items.text: Ask a question about the stated evidence before inferring a motive.
Provide a usable response option for a learning exercise.
The only evidence packet is unavailable to a participant’s reading setup.
No one knows who can change the proposed design.
An individual raises a protected-class discrimination allegation.
Participants want the group to decide a private eligibility appeal.

lessons.next: Next, distinguish an account from the explanation attached to it.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Priya prepares a staff learning discussion about a service notice. Her draft plan requires each participant to share a personal racial experience and promises complete confidentiality. The materials use a real recipient’s identifying record. One employee asks for a practice alternative and a readable packet before the meeting. Priya has authority to revise the learning plan but not to create a new information policy.
scenario.prompt: How should Priya revise the arrangement?
options: Use appropriate practice material, remove compulsory disclosure, explain actual limits and coordinate usable preparation.
Require the account because everyone must participate identically.
Cancel all equity learning because the original arrangement has problems.
responses: This corrects the identified gaps while preserving a practical learning purpose.
Identical demands can impose unnecessary private disclosure and do not establish usable participation.
The problems call for responsible redesign and guidance, not the loss of a suitable learning opportunity.

lessons.transfer: Draft two conduct expectations, a usable participation option and a pause route for an invented work discussion.

move.control: You can prepare information and explain roles, limits and participation arrangements.
move.failure: A discussion requires private disclosure, confuses discomfort with misconduct or promises limits it cannot honor.
move.next: Check the materials, roles and concern route before a relevant conversation begins.

lessons.title: Separate observations, interpretations and missing evidence
lessons.summary: Examine a claim carefully without dismissing an experience or declaring a cause prematurely.
lessons.objective: Separate a practice observation from its proposed explanation.
objectives: Separate a practice observation from its proposed explanation.
Ask a neutral question that tests a claim without making a participant defend a whole community.
Identify what further evidence a work decision needs.
takeaways: Describe what the information establishes before deciding what it means.
Experience can reveal a question without proving every explanation.
Missing information is neither agreement nor absence of a barrier.
lessons.statement: Careful inquiry can take an account seriously and still ask what it supports, what it leaves open and what the work needs next.

image.caption: Listening and careful questions help distinguish an account from an assumption.

intro.heading: What does the claim actually establish?
intro.body:
A participant says an application process feels less welcoming to people from a particular community. Another replies that the instructions are identical for everyone, so the concern cannot be about equity. Neither statement completes the analysis. The first account may reveal a relevant barrier to examine. The second describes uniform instructions, but uniformity does not establish how people encounter or use them. A facilitator can take the account seriously without announcing an unsupported cause, and can examine the rule without treating it as proof of equal access.

Separate the observation, interpretation and unanswered question. An observation may come from a record, a specific event or a reported experience. Its source and scope matter. An interpretation proposes why the event occurred or what it means. A useful question asks what further evidence could distinguish explanations or improve a decision. This distinction prevents a conversation from becoming a competition between absolute conclusions.

Ask questions that are specific and neutral. “Which step created the difficulty, and what information would help us understand it?” examines the process. “Why is your community unwilling to follow instructions?” supplies a group explanation and asks a person to defend it. A racial or cultural category is not an account of an individual’s motivation. Participants can contribute their knowledge without becoming representatives, data sources for private records or subjects of an improvised IDI assessment.

Different forms of evidence answer different questions. An approved aggregate report may identify a progression pattern. A direct account may explain how an instruction was encountered. A process walkthrough may show that a contact route is unclear. None alone supplies every part of the explanation. Use appropriate data expertise and authorized information practices when combining them. The leader should not collect identities from names or expand access to private records to fill a gap quickly.

At the end of this part of the discussion, name what is established and what needs work. A question about an access barrier may justify testing the instruction or seeking relevant perspectives before deciding among options. If the account raises a formal concern, preserve its actual route. Do not require the participant to prove the whole systemic explanation before the group can examine a practical issue, and do not present respectful inquiry as a completed formal determination.

lessons.keyStatement: Take experience seriously while keeping conclusions and questions within the evidence.

items.title: “The same rule means the same experience”
items.body: A uniform rule can be relevant, but its wording does not establish access in use. Ask how people encounter the process and where they face difficulty. The review may confirm that a step works or identify a barrier. Do not treat either outcome as predetermined merely because the procedure appears identical on paper.

items.title: “One account proves the whole cause”
items.body: A specific account can show an effect or expose a question that other records missed. Its importance does not make it evidence of every cause or every person’s experience. Describe the scope accurately and seek other relevant information. A careful limit should not become a reason to erase the account or demand an impossible universal proof.

items.title: “No response means no concern”
items.body: Nonresponse may reflect several conditions, including timing, unclear purpose, access or satisfaction. The facilitator cannot select the most reassuring explanation without evidence. Keep the missing perspective visible and identify an appropriate invitation or information check. Do not turn an unknown into a favorable measure or a personal commitment judgment.

tabs.label: An account
tabs.body: A participant’s account can reveal how a process was experienced and where to ask a better question. Invite the relevant detail without requiring a private history or a claim to represent everyone. Treat it as scoped evidence, not a nuisance because it differs from the report or a complete explanation merely because it is vivid.

tabs.label: A pattern
tabs.body: A documented pattern may show a difference across groups under defined conditions. Check definitions, population, period and privacy before interpreting it. A difference can warrant inquiry while its cause remains uncertain. Neither automatically declare discrimination nor dismiss the pattern because the policy wording is uniform; obtain appropriate review and process evidence.

tabs.label: A process check
tabs.body: A walkthrough can show whether an instruction, route or arrangement is usable for the task being examined. It can help test a proposed barrier without determining every historical cause. State what was checked and by whom through suitable information practices. A small test informs a bounded decision; it cannot certify universal fairness.

check.question: An approved report shows a group difference, and one participant describes a related access difficulty. What is the strongest interpretation?
check.correct: Both sources may inform a process inquiry, but their scope and missing evidence must be examined before declaring a cause or choosing a response.
wrong: The two sources automatically prove one cause for every person.
The account should be ignored because only numerical information matters.
Uniform instructions prove the reported difference cannot reflect any barrier.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response preserves relevant evidence and uncertainty while connecting inquiry to the work.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Combining two sources does not automatically establish a universal cause. Dismissing experience loses knowledge about how a process is used. Uniform wording cannot prove the absence of a barrier. Examine each source’s scope and identify the information needed for a bounded decision.

items.text: The approved report shows a difference for this population and period.
A participant reports that the contact instructions were unclear.
The difference may relate to where people encounter the notice.
Every person in the group must have the same reason for leaving.
The report does not explain why people stopped at that stage.
No direct account covers use of the alternate contact route.

lessons.next: Next, make room for different views without requiring a debate over anyone’s dignity.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Tomas facilitates review of a proposed contact instruction. An authorized aggregate report shows a racial difference in progression through one process stage. Colleague Nia describes an unclear contact route, while another staff member says equal wording proves equal experience. Tomas has no evidence of every person’s reason and no authority to access private case histories for the meeting.
scenario.prompt: Which facilitation response improves the inquiry?
options: Announce that one cause is proven and close questions.
Ignore Nia’s account because the report is numerical.
Separate the scoped pattern and account, ask about the process step and identify further authorized evidence needed.
responses: This overstates the evidence and forecloses useful examination.
The account can reveal how a step is encountered; dismissing it loses relevant knowledge.
This takes both sources seriously, preserves limits and gives the group a practical next inquiry.

lessons.transfer: Write an observation, a possible interpretation and a neutral question using an invented process example.

move.control: You can keep claims scoped and identify what the decision needs to know next.
move.failure: The group turns uniform wording into reassurance or treats a partial account as universal proof.
move.next: Before recording a conclusion, identify its evidence, scope and unanswered question.

lessons.title: Respond to disagreement without assigning group roles
lessons.summary: Support a clear exchange of reasons while addressing stereotypes, interruptions and unequal participation.
lessons.objective: Rewrite a group-based assumption as an examinable work question.
objectives: Rewrite a group-based assumption as an examinable work question.
Choose a facilitation response to an interruption without requiring the affected person to teach or forgive.
Distinguish a disagreement over evidence from an attack on a participant’s identity.
takeaways: Ask people to explain reasoning rather than defend an assigned group role.
Manage the discussion process instead of rewarding the loudest voice.
Respectful inquiry does not require treating every statement as equally sound.
lessons.statement: The facilitator can preserve disagreement about the work and still set a clear boundary around stereotypes and personal attacks.

image.caption: A useful exchange gives different reasons room without assigning a representative role.

intro.heading: Keep the disagreement specific
intro.body:
A participant challenges a proposed change because it may increase workload. Another calls the challenge resistance to equity. The disagreement may involve a real tradeoff, a misunderstanding or an assumption that needs examination. A facilitator should not decide the person’s motivation from the objection alone. Ask what work concern the participant is raising and what evidence supports it. The group can then compare the concern with the intended benefit and examine possible alternatives.

Not every statement is simply another legitimate perspective. A racial stereotype or identity-based attack can undermine participation and may raise a formal concern. Address the statement or conduct clearly without turning the affected person into the group’s educator. A leader can say that the group will not use a racial generalization as evidence and ask for a work-specific claim. This sets a process boundary without announcing an unauthorized legal finding about the speaker.

Participation may be uneven for reasons the facilitator cannot infer from silence. A confident speaker can occupy much of the discussion; others may need time, a clearer question or another appropriate way to contribute. Manage interruptions and pace, and invite scoped views without requiring anyone to speak. Do not call on a colleague to deliver the position of a whole community. Allow a person to say that they have no contribution at this point without using that response to assign a cultural-development label.

Clarify what is being challenged. A question about the evidence for an option is different from telling someone their identity makes them unreliable. Asking for the basis of a proposed cause can improve analysis; requiring a participant to prove that their personal experience deserves respect changes the task. Keep attention on claims, process and work effects. Seek responsible support when the interaction becomes unsuitable for the facilitator’s role or when formal handling is needed.

End a disagreement with an accurate account, not forced consensus. Participants may identify a shared fact, a remaining difference and an information need. Those are useful outputs even if people do not endorse the same option. The decision owner remains responsible for the next work step and an explanation of how reasons were considered. A respectful conversation should not rewrite silence or reluctant assent as agreement.

inThisLesson: Ask what concern is being raised.
Distinguish a work question from a stereotype.
lessons.keyStatement: Keep reasons discussable while refusing to make identity a substitute for evidence.

items.title: A concern becomes a motive label
items.body: “You resist equity” may skip the actual issue. Ask which workload, access or decision concern is being raised and what evidence supports it. The response may reveal a misconception or a genuine constraint to examine. Address the reasoning and its effect without using a label to avoid the analytical work.

items.title: A stereotype becomes the explanation
items.body: A statement about what an entire racial group supposedly wants is not evidence of each person’s experience. Name the problem with the generalization and return to scoped information. Do not ask the affected colleague to refute it on behalf of everyone. Preserve appropriate formal duties if the statement also raises a workplace concern.

items.title: The loudest voice closes the issue
items.body: Confidence and repeated interruption do not establish the strongest reasoning. Restate the question, manage turns and offer suitable ways to contribute. Record an unresolved difference accurately rather than demanding that quiet participants endorse the dominant view. The group may need further information, not a louder or longer version of the same claim.

tabs.heading: Compare three responses to a disputed claim

tabs.label: Clarify the reason
tabs.body: Ask for the work-specific concern and its evidence. This can turn an accusation into an issue the group can examine, such as a workload dependency. Clarification does not excuse a stereotype or make an unsupported claim sound. It provides a route to reasoning when the discussion can appropriately continue.

tabs.label: Set a conduct boundary
tabs.body: Address an interruption or group generalization directly and calmly. Explain that the group will examine evidence without assigning identity-based motives or representative roles. The affected person need not supply a lesson or a forgiveness statement. Use the responsible reporting route if formal duties arise; the conversation is not a tribunal.

tabs.label: Name the unresolved issue
tabs.body: If reasons still differ, record what remains uncertain and what evidence may help. Forced consensus can hide the very tradeoff the decision owner needs to see. An accurate account permits a responsible decision even when participants do not agree. Do not report silence or agreement under pressure as voluntary support.

check.question: A participant says a whole racial community does not value the service, then asks one colleague to confirm it. What should the facilitator do?
check.correct: Reject the generalization as evidence, remove the representative demand and return to a scoped work question with appropriate process handling if needed.
wrong: Ask the colleague to defend the entire community before discussion continues.
Accept the statement as equally reliable merely because it is someone’s viewpoint.
Assign the speaker an intercultural-development orientation from the remark.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response protects participation and analytical quality without demanding group representation or making a personal assessment.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Requiring a colleague to defend a whole community repeats the burden. A viewpoint does not become reliable evidence simply because it is expressed. A single remark cannot supply an assessed developmental orientation. Address the statement and conduct, restore the work question and follow actual duties where a formal concern arises.

items.text: The option may require staff time the plan has not accounted for.
The report does not establish why people leave this stage.
The facilitator stops interruptions and offers a written response option.
A colleague is not required to speak for every community member.
People from that background never want these services.
The objection proves the employee has a particular IDI orientation.

lessons.next: Next, distinguish a learning response from formal concern handling.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Jordan chairs a review of outreach options. Staff member Eli raises a workload question. Another participant calls Eli resistant, interrupts the answer and says a racial community simply does not value the service. They ask colleague Mara to confirm the community view. Jordan has enough time to restate the question and must follow responsible procedures for any actual workplace concern.
scenario.prompt: What response best improves the discussion?
options: Ask Eli to explain the workload evidence, stop the interruption and reject the racial generalization without requiring Mara to represent a community.
Ask Mara to defend the community so the group can decide which person is right.
Rate everyone’s intercultural orientation and use the scores to settle the dispute.
responses: This addresses process and reasoning while preserving appropriate formal handling; it does not require agreement with the unsupported claim.
That imposes an unfair representative role and substitutes a personal debate for a work inquiry.
An improvised rating is unsupported and does not examine the workload or outreach evidence.

lessons.transfer: Write a calm response to a practice interruption that names the conduct issue and returns to a specific evidence question.

move.control: You can manage the process and reject identity-based generalizations as a substitute for evidence.
move.failure: Participants must defend assigned groups or the strongest voice turns silence into agreement.
move.next: In the next appropriate discussion, distinguish the work concern, conduct boundary and unresolved information need.

lessons.title: Preserve formal responsibilities when a concern arises
lessons.summary: Recognize when a discussion needs a protected reporting route, appropriate support or another decision-maker.
lessons.objective: Identify a practice statement that requires a manager’s formal reporting response.
objectives: Identify a practice statement that requires a manager’s formal reporting response.
Explain a privacy boundary without promising absolute confidentiality or dismissing the concern.
Retain a suitable general work question while routing an individual matter.
takeaways: A learning conversation does not replace complaint or investigation procedures.
Managers retain actual reporting duties when concerns arise.
A useful referral protects the person and keeps responsibility visible.
lessons.statement: The discussion’s purpose cannot be used to delay a formal duty or make personal disclosure the price of an appropriate response.

image.caption: A clear response distinguishes a general work issue from an individual concern needing another route.

intro.heading: Know when the purpose changes
intro.body:
A participant describes an actual protected-class harassment or discrimination concern during an equity discussion. The facilitator may be tempted to keep talking so the meeting can resolve the conflict. That changes the task. A staff learning conversation is not an investigation, a required confrontation or a group vote on whether an allegation is valid. Preserve the relevant formal process and explain the next responsible step without collecting unnecessary detail in front of the group.

MMB Policy 1436 sets actual responsibilities for covered managers and supervisors. They must take reports seriously, respond appropriately, immediately report allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer, and follow agency complaint and investigation procedures. They must not wait for a course activity, an informal conversation or the next scheduled debrief before fulfilling that duty. Other concerns may fall under different policies or routes; use current scope and responsible guidance rather than assuming one policy covers everything.

Explain information boundaries honestly. Do not promise absolute confidentiality, disclose another person’s information or ask participants to post a detailed personnel account in learning notes. Pause unnecessary identifying discussion and arrange appropriate handling through approved channels. A person should not have to narrate their case to the group to make a process barrier worthy of examination. Formal reporting and the appropriate practical response can proceed without turning the meeting into a public record of every private fact.

The general work question may still be useful. A concern about a remark during review might also reveal unclear turn-taking or how evidence is dismissed. The group can examine a suitable non-identifying process issue without determining the individual allegation. A practical change does not resolve that allegation automatically. Keep the action, authority and records separate so neither the learning work nor the formal route disappears behind an assurance that everything has been handled.

The leader’s follow-through also must avoid retaliation. Actual law and policy determine protected activity and applicable responsibilities. Do not make appropriate support conditional on withdrawing a concern, staying silent or forgiving another person. Use responsible advice for real situations and base legitimate work decisions on their proper evidence and authority. The course teaches the boundary, not the outcome of an actual case.

inThisLesson: Keep general improvement and case handling distinct.
lessons.keyStatement: Follow the actual concern route promptly; a discussion cannot substitute for the responsible process.

items.title: “Let the group decide whether it happened”
items.body: Group agreement cannot confer investigation authority or establish a fair finding. Preserve appropriate reporting and records, and do not pressure people to provide testimony in a learning activity. The responsible process may require facts the meeting cannot obtain appropriately. A suitable general design question can remain without the group adjudicating an individual concern.

items.title: “Try mediation before reporting”
items.body: Do not invent an informal prerequisite for a formal route. Manager duties under the applicable policy continue to apply, including immediate reporting where Policy 1436 governs. A conversation or mediation may be appropriate in a particular process, but its suitability and choice need responsible guidance. Learning should not add a barrier to exercising actual rights.

items.title: “A process change closes the case”
items.body: Improving turn-taking may address one meeting barrier, but it does not determine a harassment allegation or remove required handling. Explain the practical correction and the separate formal route accurately. This avoids both neglecting a useful improvement and overstating what it resolves. Keep personal records and decisions within their approved settings.

tabs.label: Practical improvement
tabs.body: The leader can examine a suitable work arrangement, such as how the chair preserves a contribution during review. State the effect, correction and owner within authority. That work can proceed while another route handles a concern. Do not describe the improvement as proof that the allegation is resolved or as a condition for using the formal process.

tabs.label: Formal handling
tabs.body: An actual protected-class concern requires the applicable reporting and agency process. For managers and supervisors, Policy 1436 includes immediate reporting to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Preserve the appropriate records and avoid a group investigation. A facilitator’s confidence does not create decision powers or make a learning reflection an authorized finding.

tabs.label: Learning practice
tabs.body: The course can use practice details to teach how to recognize and explain these boundaries. It cannot determine a real person’s case, assign culpability or replace required training. Staff can seek consultant guidance on the work while retaining their own responsibilities. Keep learning responses separate from personnel documentation and information the responsible office must handle.

check.question: A supervisor hears an allegation of protected-class discrimination during a learning discussion. What is the appropriate next response?
check.correct: Take it seriously, immediately report it to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436, and follow current agency procedures without investigating through the group.
wrong: Wait until the group votes on whether the account is convincing.
Require the person to confront the alleged actor before any reporting.
Keep the matter entirely in course notes to preserve the informal tone.
check.feedbackCorrect: The supervisor preserves the actual reporting duty and appropriate process, rather than turning the learning discussion into an investigation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A group vote cannot decide whether a formal report should occur. Compulsory confrontation adds a prerequisite the learning activity has no authority to create. Course notes are not the approved record for an actual personnel concern. Follow immediate manager reporting and current agency procedures while limiting unnecessary shared detail.

items.text: Immediately report a covered allegation to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer.
Follow the actual agency complaint and investigation procedure.
Clarify turn-taking for a future review without personal case details.
Test whether the new arrangement allows relevant evidence to be considered.
Require a public forgiveness statement before the report proceeds.
Use a team vote as a substitute for the formal finding.

lessons.next: Next, connect discussion findings to a responsible action and review.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Ren facilitates a learning discussion on review participation. Employee Casey raises an actual allegation of protected-class discrimination and begins describing personnel details. Ren proposes a public debate followed by a forgiveness statement so the meeting can continue. A non-identifying question about how contributions enter review is also relevant. This practice exercise does not determine whether an actual policy violation occurred.
options: Let the discussion vote on the case and keep records in the learning file.
Pause unnecessary detail, fulfill immediate reporting and current procedures, and retain a suitable general process question separately.
Ignore the allegation because the meeting was scheduled for learning.
responses: This creates an unauthorized adjudication and inappropriate record path.
This takes the concern seriously without exposing more information or losing a useful improvement question.
The scheduled purpose does not erase a supervisor’s actual duties when a concern arises.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice response explaining the immediate responsible route and one non-identifying work question that can remain.

move.control: You can fulfill your actual reporting duties and keep learning separate from formal case handling.
move.failure: A discussion delays reporting, compels confrontation or publicly decides an individual concern.
move.next: Before facilitating, confirm the relevant agency routes and explain information limits accurately.

lessons.title: Turn the conversation into action and honest follow-through
lessons.summary: Record what the discussion established, what remains uncertain and who carries the next work step.
lessons.objective: Write a finding and uncertainty without claiming consensus from silence.
objectives: Write a finding and uncertainty without claiming consensus from silence.
Connect an action and owner to a specific practice work barrier.
Choose evidence that checks usefulness rather than simply meeting completion.
takeaways: A discussion record should preserve the actual reasons and limits.
Action needs a responsible owner and an appropriate authority boundary.
Review both delivery and effect before claiming improvement.
lessons.statement: A worthwhile conversation leaves people able to see what the work needs next and who will carry it forward.

image.caption: Follow-through connects a discussion with a practical change and a suitable check.

intro.heading: What changed because we examined the question?
intro.body:
A discussion ends with a list of concerns and several possible changes. The leader thanks everyone and calls the meeting successful. Participation may have been valuable, but the work is not complete merely because people spoke. Record what the discussion actually established, which reasons differed and what remains unknown. Explain how those findings connect to the next decision or action. A group can produce useful inquiry without arriving at consensus.

Keep the account scoped. A suggestion is not an adopted decision; an adopted decision is not yet a delivered change; a delivered change is not automatically a demonstrated improvement. For example, staff may identify confusing contact instructions, authorize a revision and send the new wording. A suitable check still needs to examine whether people can use it at the relevant point. Do not turn those different stages into a single success label.

Assign responsibility to the real work roles. The supervisor or program owner may prepare the change, another role may authorize it, and staff may test its use through approved arrangements. The consultant can provide guidance and feedback, not silently become the person responsible for every analysis and correction. If authority is unresolved, name the decision that needs responsible review rather than making a promise on behalf of another office.

Choose evidence proportionate to the task. A practice response can show whether a learner understands the process. An actual work check needs its appropriate information, privacy and decision arrangements. Meeting counts or attendance establish activity; they do not prove barriers were removed, racial disparities changed or every participant now agrees. Missing responses should remain unknown. Relevant experience and process information may guide a next improvement without supporting a universal causal claim.

Give a response at the agreed point. Explain the action, reason, owner and remaining question in understandable language. Preserve formal concern routes and information boundaries; a summary should not expose personnel accounts to demonstrate transparency. If the action did not help, revise it or obtain further guidance. Follow-through means remaining accountable to the work effect, not requiring participants to announce that trust, comfort or agreement has been restored.

inThisLesson: Separate suggestion, decision, delivery and effect.
Name an action owner and authority.
lessons.keyStatement: Report what occurred and what it supports, then carry the next work responsibility forward.

items.title: Attendance becomes endorsement
items.body: A meeting record can show who attended without establishing agreement with every option. Record the actual recommendation, reasons and unresolved differences as appropriate. Do not pressure quiet participants to endorse a conclusion for a reassuring summary. The decision owner needs an accurate account, including what further work may be necessary.

items.title: A promise has no owner
items.body: “We will make this equitable” leaves the action and responsibility unclear. Identify a specific barrier, the proposed correction and the role that can authorize and perform it. State any unresolved requirement. A bounded action with a check is more useful than a broad promise that everyone assumes another person will carry out.

items.title: Completion becomes proof of effect
items.body: A sent document shows delivery, but does not establish that the route is understandable. Check the intended use through appropriate arrangements and explain the scope of the evidence. A small test can inform revision without proving a universal result. Missing information should prompt a suitable next question rather than reassuring language.

tabs.heading: Connect the evidence to the next decision

tabs.label: What was learned
tabs.body: State the actual observation or supported account and the question it clarified. Include different reasons and limits where relevant. The group may learn that a contact instruction lacks a clear destination without establishing every cause of a broader disparity. Accurate scope keeps the finding useful and prevents the conversation from claiming more than it examined.

tabs.label: What will happen
tabs.body: Describe the correction, responsible role and authority still needed. A recommendation may be considered without being adopted, and that distinction deserves a reasoned response. Staff do the work with optional consultant guidance. Do not make the consultant the default owner merely because they helped the group frame the question.

tabs.label: What will be checked
tabs.body: Separate evidence of delivery from evidence of usefulness. Confirm the revision occurred, then examine whether the intended task can be completed under appropriate conditions. State limitations and other influences before drawing a broader outcome claim. If the change fails, use the finding to revise the work rather than requiring participants to supply a success statement.

check.question: A team revised a contact instruction after discussion and reported that every racial access barrier is now removed. What should the account say instead?
check.correct: Describe the actual revision and an appropriate usability check with its limits, leaving broader outcome questions open unless further evidence supports them.
wrong: Make the success claim stronger because the meeting was well attended.
Treat nonresponses as confirmation that the change worked for everyone.
Ask the consultant to take over every staff task so the owner need not review it.
check.feedbackCorrect: This gives the improvement credit for what it can establish while retaining uncertainty and responsible follow-through.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Attendance does not prove the effect of a revision. Nonresponse cannot establish universal usefulness. Consultant guidance does not transfer every process owner’s work responsibility. State the delivered change, check its actual use and identify what evidence remains needed before making a broader claim.

items.text: Staff held the planned discussion.
The responsible role sent the approved revised instruction.
A suitable process check showed users could identify the next contact.
Appropriate feedback identified a remaining unclear step for revision.
No further comments prove every participant agrees.
One revision eliminated all racial barriers across the program.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to prepare and review one suitable work discussion.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Denise’s team discusses racial equity in a contact instruction. Staff revise the wording and conduct a small approved usability check that identifies the contact successfully but does not cover every relevant experience. Denise wants to report that the program eliminated racial barriers. The consultant helped frame the discussion; staff still own the change and its review. A broader outcome question remains unanswered.
scenario.prompt: Which closing account is best supported?
options: Announce that all barriers were eliminated and stop further review.
Record only the meeting count because effects are too difficult to examine.
Describe the revision, bounded check and missing perspectives, then name the staff-owned next review with optional consultant guidance.
responses: This exceeds the evidence and hides the remaining inquiry.
Activity is useful to record, but the scoped check also supplies information that can guide the work.
This preserves the demonstrated improvement, limits and real responsibility for follow-through.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a practice closing note with a finding, unresolved question, action, owner and suitable usefulness check.

move.control: You can keep the account accurate and make next responsibilities visible.
move.failure: A productive conversation becomes an unsupported success claim or a task everyone assumes belongs to the consultant.
move.next: At the agreed follow-up, report delivery and usefulness separately and revise the action where evidence shows a remaining barrier.

jobAid.subtitle: Prepare a focused conversation and connect it to responsible action.
remember: Name the work question and the real decision opportunity.
Use race-relevant evidence without group scripts or motive guesses.
Offer appropriate participation choices without compulsory private disclosure.
Managers retain immediate reporting duties under applicable Policy 1436.
Staff own analysis and action; the consultant provides guidance and feedback.
Silence, attendance and a delivered change are not universal proof of agreement or effect.

sections.heading: Before discussion
items: Describe the specific decision, choices open and responsible owner.
Prepare relevant, usable information and clarify its limits.
Explain facilitator and participant roles without representative burdens.
Agree on conduct, pause and appropriate alternative arrangements.
Confirm formal concern routes and avoid absolute confidentiality promises.

sections.heading: During discussion
items: Separate observation, interpretation and unanswered question.
Ask neutral questions about the actual process and evidence.
Manage interruptions and reject racial generalizations as evidence.
Do not require a colleague to defend a community or infer an individual IDI result.
Fulfill actual reporting responsibilities and protect unnecessary private detail.

sections.heading: After discussion
items: Record actual findings, different reasons and uncertainties.
Distinguish suggestions, authorized decisions, delivery and effect.
Name the action, owner, authority and appropriate review.
Respond to contributions without claiming every suggestion was adopted.
Use appropriate evidence to check usefulness and revise the work.

sources.title: Minnesota Office of Collaboration and Dispute Resolution — Inclusive Conflict Resolution
sources.note: Public resources support respectful, inclusive approaches to conflict. The facilitation routines are course examples, not new required agency procedures.

sources.title: Minnesota Office of Collaboration and Dispute Resolution — Bridging and Polarization
sources.note: Public learning context for connection across differences; no universal outcome or formal-case resolution is claimed.

sources.title: Minnesota DHS — Equity Policy
sources.note: Actual daily equity responsibilities and required analysis remain in place. Discussion and voluntary course completion do not substitute for the policy’s formal tool and review requirements.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited Policy 1436
sources.note: Direct source for immediate manager/supervisor reporting and responsible handling of protected-class harassment and discrimination. A learning meeting does not investigate or determine a case.

sources.title: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — Retaliation
sources.note: Federal guidance distinguishes protected activity from legitimate workplace responsibilities. A specific matter depends on its facts and responsible agency advice; the course does not adjudicate it.
